To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the brainstem can tolerate high doses of radiation, but (2) the tolerance is a steep function of the volume receiving high doses, (3) the maximum dose is less important than the volume receiving high dose, (4) patients with a history of diabetes or hypertension have a higher risk of developing radiation induced brainstem injury, and (5) the extent of surgery is a major risk factor.

brainstem tolerance to fractionated conformal radiotherapy is a steep function of volume of the brain stem included in high-dose regions, and that the prevalence of diabetes and the extent of surgical manipulation are independent prognostic factors.

the incidence of high-grade brainstem toxicity in the treatment of skull base tumors with conformal high-dose radiation can be significantly decreased by limiting the volume of brainstem included in high dose volumes and by avoiding the presence of predisposing conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the analysis of the long-term incidence and the risk factors for brainstem tolerance to high dose radiotherapy in patients with skull base tumors.
the long-term outcome of patients with skull base tumors treated with high-dose conformal radiotherapy with respect to the incidence of brainstem injury.
the development of a new method for the treatment of the brainstem.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the risk of brainstem injury is not only a matter of dose but also a function of volume, and that the risk of toxicity is increased in patients with a history of diabetes, hypertension, and extensive surgical manipulation.

the brainstem is not a dose limiting structure in the treatment of skull base tumors with conformal radiotherapy, provided that the brainstem volume receiving > or =60 CGE is limited to less than 2 cc.
the incidence of brainstem complications can be reduced by limiting the volume of brainstem to receive 50 CGE and below, and by avoiding surgical procedures whenever possible.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the incidence of brainstem damage is low and that it can be reduced further by careful delineation and dose prescription to brainstem and avoidance of surgical procedures.
the risk of brainstem injury is significantly increased when the volume of the brain stem receiving 50 to 60 CGE exceeds 1 cm(3).
the brainstem is a dose-limiting structure for skull base irradiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the volume of brainstem exposed to high doses is the main factor determining the risk of brainstem injury in skull base radiotherapy.
it is possible to treat these tumors with a very high dose to the tumor and spare the brainstem.
the volume of the brain stem receiving high radiation doses is a better predictor of brainstem tolerance than the maximum dose to the brainstem.
